text: A drug is a chemical compound designed to produce a desired effect within a living system, such as preventing disease, restoring health, or relieving symptoms.
The field of drug discovery aims to design these molecules to achieve a specific response based on knowledge of a biological target.
Most commonly, this target is a biomolecule like a protein, whose function is modulated by the drug to provide a therapeutic benefit (Stromgaard et al. 2009; Chorghade 2006; Patrick 2013).

For almost all of human history, the discovery of new drugs was guided by a combination of luck and trial-and-error, and relied on the extraction of materials from the local environment: plants, minerals, and animal products 1 .
The 19th century marked the advent of modern drug discovery (Patrick 2013).

While still mostly relying on the isolation of active ingredients from traditional cures—e.g., morphine (Sertuerner 1817) or quinine (Pelletier 1820)—this era also witnessed the birth of modern chemistry: scientists developed the tools necessary to synthesise molecules in the laboratory, enabling them to modify natural compounds or create entirely new ones from scratch.
This new capability gave rise to the first synthetic drugs, like aspirin (Dreser 1899), and established the modern pharmaceutical industry (Urick et al. 2019).
More importantly, though, it marked a fundamental shift in perspective: from merely finding what worked to understanding why it worked.

A pioneering step in this direction was Paul Ehrlich’s early 20th-century concept of a ‘magic bullet’: the idea that a compound could be designed to kill a pathogen, without harming the host, by selectively targeting a mechanism unique to the microbe.
This principle led to the development of arsphenamine (Ehrlich et al. 1910), the first antibiotic, and laid the groundwork for the subsequent antibiotic revolution (Hutchings et al. 2019).

This concept of selective targeting was eventually broadened from external pathogens to the body’s own molecular machinery, which led to the first drugs designed with specific human biological mechanisms in mind, like beta-blockers and histamine H2 antagonists (Black, Crowther, et al. 1964; Black, Duncan, et al. 1972).

The development of these drugs constituted the first appearance of rational design: they were purposefully engineered to interact with a known biological target rather than being discovered serendipitously (Stromgaard et al. 2009).

Still, a final conceptual leap was required to arrive at the dominant paradigm in modern This traditional form of medicine is actually what gave us the word drug: it is derived from the Old French ‘drogue’, which in turn comes from the Middle Dutch ‘droge vate’, meaning ‘dry barrels’; a reference to medicinal plants preserved as dry matter (Tupper 2012). pharmacology: structure-based drug design (SBDD) aims to design molecules whose shape and chemical properties are complementary to a target’s binding site by using its 3D structure as a blueprint (Kuntz 1992).

This approach was made possible by advances in biophysical methods, particularly X-ray crystallography, which gave scientists the unprecedented ability to determine the atomic-level structure of proteins.

The method was first successfully demonstrated in the late 1980s with the design of dorzolamide (Baldwin et al. 1989; Greer et al. 1994), an inhibitor engineered to treat glaucoma by binding to the enzyme carbonic anhydrase.
SBDD’s most profound impact, however, came shortly after, with the determination of the HIV-1 protease structure in 1989 (Navia et al. 1989).

This sparked a monumental effort that led directly to the development of inhibitors like saquinavir (Roberts et al. 1990) and ritonavir (Kempf et al. 1995), which transformed HIV/AIDS from a fatal disease into a manageable condition.
Despite this enormous progress, developing new drugs remains a challenging process.
The expense of bringing a drug from discovery to market is immense, taking on average over ten years, with recent estimates placing the median cost at $1.3 billion (Wouters et al. 2020).
This is largely due to the high failure rate of candidate compounds, meaning that each successful drug must offset the financial burden of numerous unsuccessful attempts (Patrick 2013).
The reasons for these failures are multifaceted.

A 2019 study (Wong et al. 2019) reported that in Phase II of clinical trials—where a drug’s effectiveness is first tested in patients—a lack of efficacy was the primary cause of failure in over 50% of cases.
In Phase III, this figure rose to over 60%.

Although this statistic may seem to suggest that we are simply bad at designing binders, the reality is slightly more complex; failure can also stem from poor absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) properties (for instance, the drug may be destroyed by stomach acid or be unable to cross the blood-brain barrier) or the initial target identification may have been flawed, meaning that modulating the chosen biomolecule does not produce the desired therapeutic effect.
The other primary cause of failure is safety.
The same 2019 study reported that safety concerns consistently accounted for approximately 20-25% of failures across phases II and III (Wong et al. 2019).
These safety issues can be broadly divided into two categories.
The first of these is on-target toxicity, where the drug successfully binds to the target, but causes negative side effects.
This is an inherent and often predictable consequence of the drug’s primary mechanism, and is a common issue that frequently defines the maximum tolerated dose.

Off-target toxicity, on the other hand, arises from unintended interactions with other biological molecules, and can produce severe and unexpected adverse reactions that are a frequent cause of a drug’s outright termination from development (Cook 2023).

Accounting for every potential point of ADME or safety failure in clinical trials is practically impossible, not only due to the hugely complex nature of biological systems, but also because negative data from clinical trials is rarely disclosed publicly (Dickersin et al. 1993; DeVito et al. 2019; Laviolle et al. 2025).
Consequently, there is limited systematic data on the specifics of why and how frequently novel agents fail in late-stage development, making it difficult to learn from failures and reduce them.
A practical strategy to improve the overall success rate is to increase the number of high-quality candidates entering clinical trials.
The goal is to start with molecules that are already high-affinity, specific binders to the target of interest, thereby improving the odds of success from the outset.
An increasingly popular approach to this challenge, and the one adopted in this thesis, is the use of deep learning (DL) algorithms to screen and design drugs in the early stages of development.
For a deep learning model to be effective at structure-based drug design, it must master two fundamental challenges.
First, it must understand the underlying forces of intramolecular bonding; the chemistry and physics dictating the possible arrangements atoms can take within a compound.
This is necessary to produce novel compounds that are chemically valid and stable, ideally with properties similar to those in databases of existing drugs.
Second, it must learn the principles of intermolecular binding to predict or design molecules that bind effectively to a biological target.
The chapters of this thesis are organised around these two challenges.
Chapters 3 and 4 address the first challenge, focusing on deep learning methods for generating molecules that are chemically valid and replicate the distribution of known compounds.

Chapter 2 explores the second challenge of protein-ligand bonding, presenting work on a model for virtual screening and then attempting to extract learned information to inform the generation of new candidates.
A prerequisite for structure-based drug design, however, is the availability of an accurate 3D model of the target protein.

While the number of solved protein structures is growing (RCSB-PDB 2025), and prediction methods are improving (Baek et al. 2021; Z. Lin et al. 2023; Jumper et al. 2021; Abramson et al. 2024; Passaro et al. 2025), obtaining high-resolution structures for novel or complex targets remains a bottleneck.

This motivates the final results chapter of this thesis: chapter 5, where we describe an adaptation of the inference processes of two structure prediction methods (AlphaFold 2 via OpenFold (Jumper et al. 2021; Ahdritz et al. 2024), and AlphaFold 3 via Boltz-2 (Abramson et al. 2024; Passaro et al. 2025)) to directly incorporate cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) data, with the goal of providing high-quality predictions that align with experimental data.
First, though, we provide some necessary background and context to frame these research chapters.
We begin by summarising the drug discovery process, focusing on the early stages that this thesis falls within.

We then provide a brief overview of the machine learning (ML) methods used across the different projects within this thesis, and finally describe how computational, and in particular ML-based, methods have been used to screen and design new compounds up until now.
Finally, we outline the structure and key contributions of this thesis.
Small molecule drugs are the most conventional class of pharmaceuticals.
They are organic compounds generally defined by a molecular weight of less than 1000 daltons (Da) (Dougherty et al. 2011).
Their small size and balanced physicochemical properties allow them to cross cell membranes and reach intracellular targets such as kinases (Chhabra 2021).
These features also support oral bioavailability (Patrick 2013).

This potential for oral dosing and intracellular target access, combined with their stability, and relatively easy, cheap synthesis, are key reasons for their historical dominance in medicine (Patrick 2013; Makurvet 2021).

While the market shares of peptides and biologics are expanding (Healthcare 2022), small molecules still make up a comfortable majority of new drugs; in 2024, for instance, they accounted for 32 of the 50 novel drugs (64%) approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) (Mullard 2025).
Despite being the most simple of the different drug types, each approval marks a successful journey through the lengthy, costly, and high-risk drug discovery and development pipeline.
We elaborate on this pipeline below.
This section provides a brief overview of the small molecule drug discovery pipeline2 , before delving into the stages most relevant to this thesis.
As illustrated in Figure 1.2, the process can be depicted as a linear sequence of stages from target identification through to clinical trials.
In practice, this process is highly iterative, and characterised by a high rate of attrition, where the vast majority of projects fail to advance from one stage to the next (Cook 2023).
Briefly, the journey begins with target identification and validation, in which the biological mechanism to be targeted is found and tested.
Following this, the hit identification stage aims to find initial molecules, or ‘hits’, that can modulate the target’s activity.
These hits then enter the hit-to-lead and lead optimisation stages, where iterative chemical modifications improve key properties.
Promising lead compounds then undergo preclinical testing before potentially advancing to human clinical trials.
The work presented in this thesis falls within the target validation, hit identification and hit-to-lead stages of the drug discovery pipeline.
We go into more detail on these below.

This next phase of the drug design pipeline aims to use knowledge of the validated target to identify a viable chemical starting point, or ‘hit’.
Hit identification strategies can be broadly divided into screening and designing approaches, with fragment-based methods occupying a space between the two.
Screening approaches aim to discover active molecules from large collections.
High-throughput screening (HTS) evaluates libraries of hundreds of thousands to millions of compounds against the target in biochemical or cellular assays.
While it can reveal unexpected chemotypes, HTS is resource-intensive, generates many false positives, and typically yields very low hit rates (between 0.01% and 0.14% (T. Zhu et al. 2013)).

The computational counterpart to HTS, virtual screening (VS), evaluates large in silico libraries of molecules to prioritise a smaller, more promising subset for experimental testing (see section 1.4.2 for a more thorough introduction to VS).
In contrast to screening, design approaches instead focus on rationally constructing molecules to complement the target.
Medicinal chemists may design new compounds guided by the features of existing binders (ligand-based design) or by directly analysing the target binding pocket (structure-based design).
Computational de novo design methods parallel these strategies, algorithmically generating novel molecules predicted to have high affinity and selectivity for the binding site (see section 1.4.3).

Fragment-based drug design (FBDD) represents an intermediate strategy that identifies high-quality chemical starting points by screening collections of very small molecules, or fragments, which typically have a molecular weight below 300 Da (Howard et al. 2015).
Because these fragments are so small, their binding affinity for a target is usually weak, often in the millimolar (10−3 ) to micromolar (10−6 ) range (Zartler et al. 2008).
This necessitates the use of highly sensitive biophysical techniques for screening, such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) or X-ray crystallography.
Although they bind weakly, successful fragments are highly efficient binders; they form strong interactions relative to their small size.
This high-quality molecular recognition makes them excellent starting points for chemical elaboration.
Using the 3D structure of the fragment-protein complex as a guide, chemists evolve these initial hits into more potent lead compounds.
This can be achieved by extending the fragment with new functional groups to engage with adjacent regions on the protein surface, a strategy known as fragment growing.

Alternatively, two different fragments which bind in a similar region can be connected through fragment linking, or a single new molecule can be designed that incorporates the key features of multiple overlapping fragments in a process called fragment merging.

Since its adoption in the 1990s, FBDD has proven highly successful, leading to multiple approved drugs such as vemurafenib, venetoclax, and erdafitinib (Souers et al. 2013; Tsai et al. 2008; S. Wang, Burgess, et al. 2020).

These hit-identification strategies are not mutually exclusive and are frequently combined: for example, the chemical structures of hits from a high-throughput screen might be used to build a pharmacophoric profile (a 3D map of the essential features a molecule needs to bind to the target) for generative design, or virtual screening used to prioritise designed compounds for synthesis and experimental testing.
Identified, confirmed hits are not yet drugs.
They are merely starting points that must be refined through two subsequent phases: hit-to-lead (H2L) and lead optimisation (LO).

The H2L phase aims to convert a promising hit into a ‘lead’ by exploring the surrounding chemical space to establish a robust structure-activity relationship (SAR) and improve initial potency and drug-like properties.

The subsequent LO phase is a more intensive, multi-parameter optimisation process that aims to polish the lead compound into a preclinical candidate, balancing high potency and selectivity with a favourable ADME-T profile (Patrick 2013; Stromgaard et al. 2009).
This entire optimisation process is driven by the iterative design-make-testanalyse (DMTA) cycle.

In each cycle, new compound ideas are designed, synthesised, and evaluated in a panel of biological and physicochemical assays, and the resulting data is interpreted to inform the next round of design.
The design and analysis stages of this cycle rely heavily on the ligand-based and structure-based paradigms discussed previously.
In a ligand-based approach, the DMTA cycle is guided by interpreting the SAR from tested compounds.

Quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) models might be built to predict the potency of new designs, or a pharmacophore model might be refined to better understand the features required for activity: chemists make iterative changes to the molecule and learn from the resulting data.
The cycle becomes more efficient and rational if a high-resolution target structure is available.
In this structure-based approach, chemists can directly visualise how molecules interact with the target.
For example, if a compound binds weakly, the structure may reveal a nearby hydrophobic pocket that is not being filled.
The next design can rationally add a group to occupy that pocket.
If a molecule is rapidly metabolised, the structure of a metabolic enzyme might show how to block the site of metabolism without disrupting on-target binding.
SBDD thus provides an atomic-level roadmap for solving this multi-parameter optimisation challenge (Patrick 2013; Stromgaard et al. 2009).
The drug discovery stages detailed above present complex challenges.
Navigating the vastness of chemical space and understanding intricate structure-activity relationships are major bottlenecks that make this process slow and resource-intensive.
These problems are particularly well-suited to ML, which has shown promise at learning from complex data.
The following section will introduce the fundamental ML concepts that are applied to these challenges throughout this thesis.

How they are actually applied to the problems described in section 1.2 will be reviewed in section 1.4.
ML is a subfield of artificial intelligence (AI) focused on the automated detection of patterns in data, which enables computer systems to uncover key insights and predict outcomes.
While the field is vast, most approaches share a common strategy: an algorithm learns to identify patterns from input data without being explicitly programmed.
The primary objective is for the resulting model to generalise from this experience and accurately interpret new, unseen inputs.
The landscape of ML is complex, with methods often stratified by paradigm, architecture, or application.
This can lead to confusion, particularly with terms like ‘AI’, ‘ML’, and ‘DL’ that are often used interchangeably despite their distinct meanings.
To help clarify these relationships and provide a conceptual map, we present a flowchart in Figure 1.3 outlining the key methods under the umbrella of AI.
Following this flowchart, we will begin by introducing the foundational supervised learning paradigm.
We then move to the fundamental model architecture that forms the basis of modern deep learning: neural networks.
From there, we will explore the two architectures most commonly used in SBDD: convolutional neural networks and graph neural networks.
Finally, we will shift our focus from predictive models to the generative domain with an introduction to diffusion models.
This section is not intended as a comprehensive review of all of these topics; we simply aim to introduce the paradigms, architectures, and applications that are employed in the later chapters.

Supervised learning is a paradigm where the model learns a mapping function from input variables (X) to an output variable (y) based on a set of labelled training examples, D = {(xi , yi )}N the true function f such that y = f (x).
The model, parametrised by weights θ, learns to make predictions ŷ = f (x; θ) by minimising a loss function L(ŷ, y), which quantifies the error between the prediction and the ground truth.
This is typically an optimisation problem aimed at finding the optimal parameters θ∗ that minimise the expected loss over the entire data distribution.
In practice, this expectation is approximated by the empirical mean over the training data, which provides the objective used for gradient-based optimisation.
The primary tasks within supervised learning are regression, where y is a continuous value, and classification, where y is a discrete category.

As illustrated in Figure 1.3, diffusion models are not tied to a specific network architecture, but are instead a class of deep generative models.
These models aim to approximate the data distribution and generate new samples that are statistically indistinguishable from the training data.

Earlier approaches such as adversarial models (where a generator and discriminator compete to produce increasingly realistic samples) dominated generative modelling for several years, but were often limited by unstable training dynamics and mode collapse.
In contrast, diffusion models benefit from stable, likelihood-based training and have achieved state-of-the-art performance across a range of domains (Dhariwal et al. 2021; Salimans et al. 2022).

A protein’s biological role is inseparable from its three-dimensional structure.
This structure is determined by how its chain of amino acid residues folds, and dictates its ability to interact with specific binding partners such as ions, drugs, or other proteins.

We split the challenge of obtaining protein structures into different approaches: fully in silico structure prediction methods, and approaches relying on experimental methods like cryo-EM alongside ML.

Before turning to structure prediction, it is important to distinguish it from the protein folding problem: the former refers to the computational task of inferring a protein’s three-dimensional structure from its amino acid sequence, whereas the latter concerns the physical process by which a polypeptide chain adopts its native conformation.
Although the two are often conflated (Lewis 2023), it is structure prediction that has undergone dramatic advances in recent years, largely due to deep learning.
These models take as input the amino acid sequence of a protein and produce a predicted structure.
The field was transformed by the advent of AlphaFold2, with subsequent progress driven both by its successor AlphaFold3 and by open-source frameworks such as OpenFold and Boltz-2.
The core principles behind these approaches are outlined below.

AlphaFold2 The AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al. 2021) process begins with a multiple sequence alignment (MSA), which captures evolutionary relationships between the target protein sequence and similar ones found in nature.

This is processed into three key data structures: a single representation encoding features for each individual residue, an MSA representation capturing evolutionary patterns, and a pair representation, a grid where each cell stores information about the spatial relationship between a specific pair of amino acids.
These representations are the inputs for the system’s core component, the evoformer.
This block iteratively updates both the MSA and pair representations using attention mechanisms.

This facilitates a ‘cross-talk’ where evolutionary information from the MSA informs the geometric predictions in the pair representation, and vice versa, allowing the model to infer which amino acids are likely to be in close contact.
These refined representations then pass to the structure module, which builds the explicit 3D structure.

This module operates on a novel frame representation of the protein backbone, where each amino acid residue is treated as a rigid body with its own local coordinate system (a frame, defined by a rotation and translation).
This equivariant representation ensures that transformations applied to the input (like rotating the entire molecule) result in an equivalent transformation of the output.
The module iteratively refines the positions and orientations of these frames, using the geometric constraints learned by the evoformer to position each residue relative to all others.
The final 3D coordinates are then generated from these optimised frames, producing a physically realistic geometry.
AlphaFold3 AlphaFold3 (Abramson et al. 2024) is an architectural evolution of AlphaFold 2, moving from a protein-specific predictor to a general biomolecular structure prediction engine.
Its core pipeline consists of an input processing stage, a recycling block built around a new pairformer module, and a generative diffusion module for structure generation.
Unlike AlphaFold2, which heavily processed an MSA throughout its main evoformer block, AlphaFold3 distils the evolutionary information into its pair representation early on.

This allows the main pairformer block to focus exclusively on refining the relationship between input components without directly operating on the MSA, simplifying the architecture and centralising the flow of information.
The model’s increased generality stems from a fundamental change in its input representation.
While AlphaFold2 used tokens for 20 amino acids, AlphaFold3 employs an expanded, unified system that represents proteins, DNA, RNA, and smallmolecule ligands.
Proteins and nucleic acids are tokenised at the residue/nucleotide level, while ligands and other molecules are represented as a collection of individual heavy-atom tokens.
These diverse inputs are processed into a single representation (1D features per token) and a pair representation (2D features for every pair of tokens).

This unified framework allows the pairformer to learn interactions between any combination of biomolecules (such as protein-ligand or protein-DNA) by updating the pair representation through triangular attention mechanisms, which enforce geometric consistency.
The most major architectural change in AlphaFold3, however, is the replacement of AlphaFold2’s structure module with a diffusion module.

Instead of predicting a set of rigid frames for each residue, the diffusion model begins with a random 3D cloud of atoms and iteratively denoises it into a physically plausible structure, conditioned on the refined pair representation from the pairformer.
This generative approach directly produces all-atom coordinates without enforcing rotational and translational equivariance, a core principle of AlphaFold2.

This allows for more accurate prediction of flexible side chains, chemical modifications, and the precise geometry of non-protein molecules, marking a shift from a template-like construction to a more flexible, generative process for creating the final 3D model.

Open-source models and extensions OpenFold, Boltz-1, and Boltz-2 (Ahdritz et al. 2024; Wohlwend et al. 2024; Passaro et al. 2025) are open-source models created to replicate and expand upon the AlphaFold systems.
OpenFold is a reimplementation of AlphaFold2, renowned for releasing a full training pipeline that allowed researchers to retrain and adapt the model.
Following this, Boltz-1 was developed as the first open-source replication of AlphaFold3.
Its successor, Boltz-2, introduced the ability to predict binding affinity, meaning it can jointly predict both the structure of a complex and the strength of the interaction between its parts.

Boltz-2 also has improved accuracy over Boltz-1, and allows users to specify an experimental type (e.g. X-ray crystallography, NMR, cryo-EM) to bias its sampling towards 3D structures that are more consistent with the types of conformations typically observed by that specific technique.
Despite advances in structure prediction, the direct application of these models in drug discovery is subject to caveats.

Even for globally accurate structures, subtle but critical deviations in binding site geometry can be sufficient to mislead virtual screening and generative design algorithms (Scardino et al. 2023; Díaz-Rovira et al. 2023; Holcomb et al. 2023).
This problem is particularly acute for novel targets, where over 50% of predictions may deviate more than 2Å root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) from experimental results (Kryshtafovych et al. 2021).
A further challenge lies in evaluating the predictive models themselves, as the proprietary nature of their training data prohibits verification against potential train-test data leakage.
These issues underscore that while in silico predicted structures can serve as helpful starting points, their use necessitates caution.
The advent of highly accurate in silico predictors has greatly improved structural biology, providing hypotheses from sequence alone.
However, these models complement, rather than replace, experimental methods.

Experimental structures remain the gold standard for validation and are essential for capturing the specific, functionally relevant conformations of proteins, especially with large, dynamic complexes, or novel structures outside a model’s training scope (Škrinjar et al. 2025).
Given the continued importance of experimental data, a major focus is now on integrating ML directly into experimental workflows to overcome key bottlenecks.
A prominent example is in the interpretation of cryo-EM data.

While a cryo- EM experiment yields a three-dimensional electron density map, the subsequent process of building an atomic model into this map is often a challenge; it is timeconsuming, requires deep expertise, and can be difficult in areas of the map with low resolution or ambiguity.
This crucial step of structure elucidation is where deep learning offers potential.

We group the deep learning tools designed to automate this process into two main categories: those that interpret the map directly and those that use a hybrid approach combining the experimental data with AlphaFold.

Direct map interpretation methods The first category, direct map interpretation, encompasses methods that learn to build an atomic model de novo by treating the experimental density map as the primary source of information, often without requiring a predefined sequence.
Early deep learning approaches in this area primarily used CNNs to parse the volumetric data.
Tools like DeepTracer (Pfab et al. 2021) applied CNNs to detect key features such as Cα atoms and secondary structure elements, which were then assembled into a backbone trace.

While these approaches sped up model building, they often relied on separate downstream steps for sequence assignment and struggled in regions with fragmented or ambiguous density (e.g. very noisy or discontinuous map regions).

Recent work has suggested that while deep learning methods outperform many of the older physics-based or template-based approaches, especially at higher resolutions, performance drops off sharply at intermediate-to-low resolutions (≈4–8Å) or in local regions of low density (S. Li et al. 2025; C. Zhang et al. 2025).
More recent methods have shifted toward graph-based representations, reflecting the importance of modelling spatial and chemical relationships between atoms.
GNN-based frameworks such as ModelAngelo (Jamali et al. 2024) integrate feature detection, residue identification, and chain tracing into a single model.

By reasoning over both local density and inter-atomic connectivity, these approaches achieve higher accuracy and completeness, automating much of the previously manual model-building process even at moderate resolutions.
Nevertheless, several challenges remain.

ModelAngelo’s performance degrades at map resolutions worse than about 3.5Å, particularly for correctly assigning amino acid residues based on side-chain density and for tracing backbone connectivity in regions of weak or ambiguous density.

It also struggles with nucleotide chains: distinguishing between similar bases (e.g. the two types of purines or pyrimidines) becomes unreliable unless the map resolution is substantially better than 2.5Å (C. Zhang et al. 2025).
AlphaFold-based methods In this second category, we discuss approaches that aim to condition AlphaFold models during inference.
At the time of writing, there are two methods of this type: one built on OpenFold and the other on Boltz-2.
The first method is ROCKET (Fadini et al. 2025).
This approach reframes OpenFold as a differentiable prior for experimental structure determination.

Rather than refining coordinates directly, ROCKET keeps the pretrained prediction network intact and optimises within its prediction space, adding an experimental likelihood term that quantifies agreement with cryo-EM, cryo-ET, or X-ray data.

Because the optimisation is constrained by the structural manifold encoded in the pretrained model, the resulting fits avoid overfitting to noise and recover conformations that remain biophysically plausible, while still maximising consistency with the experimental density.
A more recent approach is CryoBoltz (Raghu et al. 2025), which conditions Boltz-2 by guiding its generative inference process with cryo-EM–derived potentials.
Global potentials encourage agreement with the overall fold present in the density, while local potentials bias fine-grained features such as loops and side chains.

In doing this, CryoBoltz injects the experimental signal directly into the sampling dynamics of Boltz-2, allowing it to generate ensembles of conformations that reflect both experimental heterogeneity and the priors learned from sequences.

Having considered methods that integrate structural priors with experimental density maps, we now turn to a complementary challenge in drug discovery: identifying small molecules that bind to a given target protein.
This problem, virtual screening, shifts the focus from the target structures to exploring the chemical space of possible binders.
As introduced in section 1.2.2.2, VS is a computational technique used primarily in the hit identification stage of drug discovery.
Much like its experimental counterpart, high-throughput screening, VS is used to search vast libraries of small molecules and prioritise those most likely to bind to a specific protein target.
The input for a VS workflow is typically a target protein structure and a collection of candidate molecules.

For each molecule, the model generates a classification (binder or non- binder), a binding pose, predicted affinity value, or some combination of these, depending on the specific predictive task it has been trained in.

In practice, VS has contributed to a number of successful drug discovery campaigns and is valued for its ability to interrogate chemical libraries on the scale of billions of compounds (Shoichet 2004; Lyu et al. 2019).
Like other hit identification methods, VS approaches can be broadly categorised into ligand-based and structure-based strategies.
Ligand-based VS exploits similarities to known active molecules, assuming that compounds sharing physicochemical features with actives are more likely to bind (Riniker et al. 2013).
Structure-based VS, by contrast, relies on the three-dimensional structure of the target protein.

The most widely used structure-based tools employ docking algorithms, which take as input the coordinates of protein and ligand atoms and generate candidate conformations of the protein–ligand complex (Morris et al. 2009; Friesner et al. 2004).
These poses are then evaluated using heuristic scoring functions that approximate binding affinity.

While often presented as energy minimisation, these functions are hybrids of empirical, knowledge-based, and physics-inspired terms designed for computational efficiency rather than strict physical accuracy (R. Wang et al. 2003; Trott et al. 2010).

Most docking workflows also approximate the receptor as rigid and treat solvation and entropy only crudely, although flexible or ensemble docking approaches can partially address this at increased computational cost (Carlson 2025; Teodoro et al. 2025).
Before the widespread adoption of ML, docking was the cornerstone of computeraided drug design, often used alongside methods such as QSAR, pharmacophore modelling, and fragment-based design.
These classical approaches laid the foundation for modern virtual screening pipelines but were limited by their reliance on predefined descriptors and simplified physics.
ML has since been applied to VS both as a replacement for and as an augmentation of docking-based scoring functions.
Early ML scoring functions were trained on hand-crafted descriptors of protein–ligand complexes using linear models or decision trees (Ballester et al. 2010).

With the rise of deep learning, convolutional neural networks operating on voxelised 3D grids became common (Ragoza, Turner, et al. 2017; Jiménez-Rosés et al. 2022), followed by graph neural networks that represent proteins and ligands as graphs and explicitly model their interactions (Lim et al. 2019; Torng et al. 2019).

More recent efforts have turned to E(3)-equivariant neural networks that respect the rotational and translational symmetries of 3D space, allowing models to better capture the geometry of binding (Townshend et al. 2022; A. Zhou et al. 2023).
Transformer-based architectures have also been explored for integrating protein sequence and structure with ligand representations (S. Luo, T. Chen, et al. 2023).

This architectural progression mirrors that in generative molecular design, where the choice of representation (grids, graphs, or full 3D structures) also influences both performance and interpretability.
Despite their promise, ML-based scoring functions are highly sensitive to the data on which they are trained.

Chemical datasets reflect a narrow and biased sample of chemical space: although the pharmacologically relevant space is estimated at around 1060 molecules (Ruddigkeit et al. 2012), available libraries are shaped by factors such as synthetic accessibility, cost, and historical precedent.

As a result, models are often evaluated on benchmarks that do not represent the diversity of possible ligands, making them vulnerable to learning dataset artefacts rather than transferable features of binding (J. Yang et al. 2020; Scantlebury, Vost, et al. 2023).
Biases can also arise during dataset curation.

For instance, in the original Database of Useful Decoys (DUD), the distribution of net charges differed substantially between actives and decoys—42% of actives were charged compared to only 15% of decoys—allowing models to inflate performance by simply labelling charged compounds as active (N. Huang et al. 2006).

This problem motivated the release of improved datasets (such as Database of Useful Decoys Enhanced (DUD-E) (Mysinger et al. 2012)), although even these remain imperfect (Scantlebury, Vost, et al. 2023; Kretschmer et al. 2025).

Evidence of learned bias is particularly clear in structure-based deep learning models: in some cases, predictive performance remains largely unchanged when the model is provided with only the ligand or only the receptor, suggesting reliance on dataset-specific correlations rather than genuine physical interactions (Wallach et al. 2018; L. Chen et al. 2019; Sieg et al. 2019).

While techniques such as ensuring diminished performance in the absence of receptor information can help (Scantlebury, Brown, et al. 2020), ultimately only interpretability methods can come close to establishing whether a model is truly learning the physics of binding.
VS remains a central tool for computational hit identification.
Classical docking provides scalability and interpretability, while modern ML architectures offer the potential for richer modelling of molecular interactions.
Yet both remain constrained by approximations in scoring functions and biases in datasets.
Addressing these limitations is essential if VS is to become a robust, generalisable approach for early-stage drug discovery.
An alternative to the VS approach, generative molecular design (GMD) algorithms automate the proposal of molecules rather than screen datasets for them.

How different GMD algorithms propose molecules varies from manually specified rulebased methods to complex deep neural network architectures trained on a collection of known molecules (M. Liu et al. 2022; Hoogeboom et al. 2022; H. Zhu et al. 2023).
Before a model can design molecules for a specific purpose (conditional generation), it must first learn the fundamental rules of what constitutes a valid, stable molecule.

This is the domain of unconditional generation, where the objective is to learn the underlying probability distribution of a large corpus of molecules and sample from it to produce novel structures that are chemically plausible.

Early approaches operated in 2D, with architectures like recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks being used to generate Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) strings, while GNNs were employed to construct molecular graphs directly by predicting nodes (atoms) and edges (bonds) (Pogány et al. 2019; Y. Yang, Ouyang, et al. 2021).
A more complex and physically relevant task is to generate molecules directly in 3D space.
This implicitly involves solving the conformer generation problem: predicting the low-energy 3D arrangement of atoms for a given 2D molecular graph.

Unconditional 3D generation models, often built on E(3)-equivariant neural networks or diffusion models (see section 1.3), learn the joint probability distribution over atom types and their 3D coordinates.
They learn to place atoms in 3D space, respecting the rotational and translational symmetries of physics.
While not directly targeted towards a biological objective, these models are the foundations upon which pocket-based conditional models are built.
In conditional generative design, a primary consideration is how to represent the protein target to guide molecule generation effectively.
This choice involves a fundamental trade-off.
Providing a model with excessive, unfiltered protein information increases the complexity of the learning task, forcing it to learn to filter out irrelevant data.
Conversely, providing simplified, pre-processed information risks introducing human bias or inadvertently omitting critical structural features.
This challenge has led to several distinct approaches, each defined by its level of structural granularity.
The most abstract approaches are shape-based, where the binding pocket is simplified to its geometric volume, often using a voxel grid or point cloud (Z. Chen et al. 2023).
This focuses on generating molecules with good steric fit but lacks chemical specificity.
A more chemically-aware strategy is to use pharmacophore-based models (Ziv et al. 2024).
Here, the binding site is described by a set of key interaction points (such as hydrogen bond donors, acceptors, and hydrophobic centres) which serve as constraints for the generative model.
These pharmacophores can be derived from the protein structure itself or from the poses of known ligands, blending structure-based and ligand-based information.

The most detailed and increasingly common approach is to use a full all-atom representation of the binding site, providing the model with the explicit 3D coordinates of all protein atoms (H. Lin et al. 2022).
This method theoretically offers the highest potential for discovering novel interactions, relying on the model to learn the underlying physics of binding directly.
De novo design refers to the creation of entirely new molecular structures from scratch.

It has evolved to feature various generative models over time, from early architectures like variational autoencoders (VAEs) and generative adversarial networks (GANs) to more recent 3D-aware methods such as CNNs (Ragoza, Masuda, et al. 2022), EGNNs (S. Luo, Guan, et al. 2022), and diffusion models (Schneuing et al. 2024).
A foundational concept underpinning many of these approaches is autoregressive generation, where the molecule is constructed sequentially.
In 1D, this involves generating a SMILES string character-by-character, with each new character conditioned on the sequence already written.
This approach also extends to 3D, where many models build a molecule atom-by-atom in the binding pocket, conditioning the placement of each new atom on the structure built so far.
This autoregressive approach has become less common with the proliferation of diffusion models, which generate all atoms simultaneously rather than sequentially.
A major challenge facing the field of generative molecular design is the assessment of binding specificity.

Current evaluation usually relies on docking scores, which may inadvertently reward the generation of promiscuous molecules; compounds with generic features that score well against a wide range of targets rather than being truly selective.
As discussed in section 1.2, off-target binding is a major cause for drugs failing clinical trials, so this must be avoided.
Finally, the field grapples with the same issues of dataset bias and generalisability that impact virtual screening.

While well-reported and publicised in VS, generalisation within generative design models remains largely untested; likely in part because the biased virtual screening tools are often the very methods used for their evaluation.

This creates a self-referential loop where models are optimised to satisfy a flawed benchmark, making it nearly impossible to determine if they can generalise to novel, out-of-distribution targets or have simply learned to exploit the biases shared with their evaluation tools.
As introduced in section 1.2.2.2, FBDD offers an alternative approach to the ‘fromscratch’ philosophy of de novo generation by building upon experimentally validated starting points.

ML has shown some promise in automating FBDD: in this approach, generative models are not tasked with exploring the entirety of chemical space, but are instead used to rationally expand upon small chemical fragments that are already known to bind to the target, thereby constraining the search to more chemically relevant regions.
As with virtual screening and de novo generative design, early methods used simple 1D and 2D representations like SMILES strings and molecular graphs.
Then, the field shifted to using 3D molecular structures with models like CNNs, EGNNs, and diffusion models.
Recently, however, the success of LLMs has brought renewed interest back to the simpler 1D text-based approaches (X. Liu et al. 2025).
A primary application of ML in FBDD is fragment elaboration.
Here, a generative model is conditioned on the 3D context of a bound fragment and the surrounding protein pocket.

New atoms are added sequentially, ‘growing’ the fragment into unoccupied regions of the binding site to form new, favourable interactions (Hadfield et al. 2022; Z. Gao et al. 2023; Y. Luo et al. 2022).
In scenarios with multiple non-overlapping fragment hits, ML can tackle the challenge of fragment linking.
Generative models are tasked with designing a chemically valid and conformationally stable linker to bridge two distinct fragments.
These algorithms must respect the geometric constraints imposed by the fragments’ exit vectors and the pocket’s shape.

Models of this type aim to generate high-quality linkers that actually form interactions with the protein, rather than just acting as simple hydrocarbon spacers (Imrie et al. 2020; Y. Yang, S. Zheng, et al. 2020; Guo et al. 2023; Y. Huang et al. 2022; Igashov et al. 2024).
Finally, fragment merging involves designing a novel scaffold that incorporates the key pharmacophoric features of multiple, overlapping fragment hits.
Most ML approaches automate this by first identifying a consensus pharmacophoric profile from the bound fragments.

This profile then serves as a set of spatial constraints to guide a generative process, tasking the model with creating a single molecule that connects these key interaction points in an optimised chemical entity (Ghorbani et al. 2023; Fu et al. 2024; Mukaidaisi et al. 2022).
This thesis presents a series of studies exploring how ML methods can be developed and adapted to better support the process of drug discovery and structural biology.
The overarching theme is the design of computational models that not only make accurate predictions, but also go some way to understanding the underlying forces of intra- and intermolecular bonding.
The first research chapter of the thesis focuses on virtual screening and fragment- based drug design.
We develop PointVS, an equivariant graph neural network trained for pose classification and affinity prediction.

By introducing stringent dataset filtering and incorporating attribution-based interpretability, we show that PointVS captures binding interactions consistent with physical interaction profiles and can be used to extract pharmacophoric information for fragment elaboration.
This enables more effective structure-guided fragment growth compared to traditional hotspot extraction methods.
The second and third research chapters of the thesis address the challenge of generating novel small molecules through diffusion-based de novo design.

Recognising that these models often struggle to produce physically plausible, druglike structures, we first explore the use of negative training data to help the model delineate valid from invalid regions of chemical space.
This approach demonstrates that incorporating both positive and negative examples improves the plausibility of generated molecules.
We then test whether simplifying the generative task can further improve results by using chemically valid fragments as building blocks instead of individual atoms.
We find that although this method is, in theory, a promising way to reduce the difficulty of de novo generation, the block-based approach introduces its own challenges.
We provide an overview of work carried out since which has attempted to implement similar, highlighting the key differences, and give an outlook based on this.
The final research chapter turns to structural biology, specifically the problem of fitting protein structures to cryo-EM density maps.
While structure prediction tools such as AlphaFold have become invaluable, they often fail on the difficult targets most relevant for cryo-EM.

We investigate conditioning strategies for incorporating cryo-EM data into AlphaFold-derived models, first within their structure modules and then through earlier interventions such as MSA subsampling.

In order to meaningfully grow a fragment into a leadlike compound, information about the protein pocket being targeted is important.

In the work presented in this chapter we investigated various computational methods for identifying hotspots: areas in protein pockets that contribute disproportionately to binding, and hence can be used to guide fragment elaboration.
This chapter first covers PointVS: an EGNN trained to perform pose classification and binding affinity prediction.

During the construction of this model, the most commonly-used benchmark for machine learning-based scoring functions, CASF16, was found to suffer from information leakage concerning almost every test structure.

With this in mind, a number of efforts were made to debias PointVS; first, performing a rigorous filtering step on the datasets that it was trained and tested on, and second, implementing an edge-attention attribution step to investigate exactly what PointVS based its predictions on.
This last step demonstrated that PointVS identifies binding interactions in at least partial agreement with a distance-based interaction profiler.

We subsequently investigated whether the attribution method could be used to identify hotspots in binding pockets when PointVS was supplied with a number of bound structures from fragment screen experiments.

We used these hotspots to perform fragment elaboration, and saw improvements in the docking scores of the resulting molecules compared to using structural information from a traditional data-based hotspot extraction method.

These results demonstrated that not only is PointVS capable of identifying important binding interactions, but also that it can be used as a tool for extracting said binding pharmacophores from a given protein target.

The work described in this chapter was carried out in contribution with Jack Scantlebury, who designed PointVS, carried out the dataset filtering, and conducted all assessments of PointVS as an MLBSF.
I prepared the code for the other attribution methods, carried out the attribution tests, and performed the fragment elaboration tests.

There are growing concerns regarding the generalisability of machine learning models, as recent research into machine learning-based scoring functions (MLBSFs) has highlighted their tendency to learn dataset biases, rather than physical interactions (Boyles et al. 2022; Sieg et al. 2019; L. Chen et al. 2019; Wallach et al. 2018).
In these cases, the MLBSFs perform less of an assessment of atomic contributions, and something more analogous to a nearest-neighbours search in ligand-pocket space.

This is useful if the application is to proteins or scaffolds with a large amount of previous binding data available, but not for new targets or ligands, as the true functional relationship governing binding is not learned.
This problem is often exacerbated by a lack of dataset filtering.
One of the most widely used benchmarks for scoring functions, both classical and machine learning-based, is the Competitive Assessment of Scoring Functions (CASF16) (Su et al. 2019).
A standard protocol for training an MLBSF is to use the PDBBind (Z. Liu et al. 2017) general set of crystal structures and binding affinities after removing the structures in CASF16.
As we found when building our scoring function, this approach suffers from information leakage concerning almost every test structure, resulting in an overestimation of the accuracy of MLBSFs.

There is an active area of research surrounding how machine learning models make predictions (Yosinski et al. 2015; Samek et al. 2015; Poelking et al. 2022; Sharma et al. 2023), a technique known as input attribution.

This is a specific application of interpretability which can be applied to MLBSFs, with the idea being that an ideal MLBSF—one which has learnt to distinguish atomic interactions, rather than just dataset biases—should be able to identify the most important binding interactions taking place in a given bound structure.
This should mean that the function predicts well on unseen targets.
In practice, the type of attribution that can be used with an MLBSF depends on its architecture.

The two prevalent deep learning architectures used as scoring functions are CNNs (Koes et al. 2013; L. Zheng et al. 2019; Y. Li et al. 2019) and GNNs (Feinberg et al. 2018; Morrone et al. 2020; Jiang et al. 2021).
Attribution for CNN-MLBSFs is limited, because spatial relationships are lost as information flows deeper into the network (Hochuli et al. 2018).

Masking—a method by which a feature is allocated a score equal to the difference between the model’s prediction made when the feature is removed from the input, and the score when it is present—can still be used, but this is computationally expensive.
Another method for performing attribution is attention analysis.
Attention mechanisms work by allocating scores to the graph’s edges, which can be thought of as indicating how much importance is ascribed to each edge by the model.
In contrast to CNNs, GNNs preserve the concept of the atom until the final layers of the network, so edges can be interrogated for information.
This is helpful in instances where an attention mechanism has been used to weight the edges, as it can give direct insight into how important the network considers each edge to be.
However, none of the current leading models for affinity prediction use attention-weighted edges for intermolecular interactions, so attribution cannot be carried out on them in this way.

If input attribution could be carried out on MLBSFs, it could be used to extract binding insights from a protein, for example, for fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD); a strategy that seeks to identify simple, small molecules (fragments) that interact with protein targets, and grow them into active leads (see chapter 1).
In order to meaningfully add atoms to these molecules, structural knowledge about the target needs to be considered.
This can be extracted from known binders, but this limits the exploration of chemical space as well as restricting the applicability of the approach to targets with known ligands.
Extracting structural information directly from the protein itself is therefore advantageous.
At the time that this work was carried out, there was only one available generative model for fragment elaboration that relies solely on protein structure (Hadfield et al. 2022).
This method uses a data-driven approach (Curran et al. 2020) to identify ‘hotspots’: regions in the protein pocket that contribute disproportionately to binding.
Currently there exists no deep learning-based tool to identify such regions.
In order to have full control over the architecture and training set of the MLBSF we perform attribution on, we built PointVS, an E(n)-equivariant graph neural network.
It is an MLBSF designed to predict both binding affinity and pose score.
We assess its performance on the CASF16 benchmark, and find it achieves comparable results to other leading scoring functions in spite of the additional filtering of the training dataset.
We then use attribution to show that the model successfully identifies binding interactions in agreement with a distance-based interaction profiler (Salentin et al. 2015).
To further investigate the power of the attribution method, we used it with fragment screen data to obtain information that can be leveraged to perform fragment elaboration.
We see that using this information extraction method results in improved docking scores compared to using a data-driven approach.
We make our code as well as our unbiased test and train splits available on GitHub at github.com/oxpig/PointVS.

PointVS is a lightweight E(n)-equivariant graph neural network, consisting of an initial projection to take the number of node features from 12 to 32, then 48 EGNN layers, followed by a global average pooling of the final node embeddings.
This is followed by a sigmoid layer which gives a label y ∈ [0, 1] during the first stage of training on pose prediction.
During finetuning on affinity data, this final layer is replaced by a randomly initiated fully connected layer and ReLU activation, which outputs y ∈ (R+ ) (see Fig 2.2).
It also uses a shallow neural network as an attention mechanism (Vaswani et al. 2017), which learns to score network edges—in this case, representing atomic interactions—by their importance.
Our EGNN takes four inputs: positions, node embeddings, edge indices, and edge embeddings.
If there are n atoms in an input structure, the positions tensor is an n × 3 tensor containing the x, y and z coordinates of each atom.
The node embeddings are an n × 12 tensor of one-hot encoded OpenBabel atom types, with a bit to distinguish between ligand and receptor atoms.
Edges are generated on-the-fly using a variable distance cutoff.
We use a cutoff of 10Å for ligand-protein edges, and 2Å for ligand-ligand and protein-protein edges.
In this way, intramolecular edges closely mimic the covalent structure of input molecules, with a much more expansive connectivity to describe intermolecular interactions.
The edge tensor is an 3 × m matrix of m edges, with one-hot encoding for ligand-ligand, ligand-receptor, and receptor-receptor interactions.
The binding pocket is defined as the collection of protein atoms within 6Å of any ligand atom; the rest of the protein is ignored.
The first of the steps made to debias PointVS was performing a thorough filtering of the datasets it was trained and tested on.

Our training dataset for pose classification was Redocked2020 (Francoeur et al. 2020) (Redocked from here on in), with the test set generated according to McNutt et al. 2021 so that classification performance could be directly compared with their work.
This test is similar to the docking power test from CASF16 (Su et al. 2019), which we also conducted.
For regression on binding affinity values, we trained a pose classifier on the Redocked set, finetuned on affinity data from the PDBBind General Set, and tested on the PDBBind Core Set.
This aimed to replicate the scoring power and ranking power tests from CASF16.
As the Core Set is a subset of the General Set, we removed Core Set structures from the training data.

In previous work by the same authors (Ragoza, Hochuli, et al. 2017), ligands from the Pocketome v17.12 (Kufareva et al. 2012) were redocked using AutoDock Vina into their cognate receptors, with an RMSD calculated between the redocked poses and the crystal pose.
Sub-2Å poses were labelled as active poses, with the rest labelled as inactive.
Further negative examples were generated adversarially: a gnina CNN trained on the original redocked dataset was used to optimise docked poses.
Optimised poses which were scored highly (> 0.9) by the trained CNN but were more than 2Å RMSD from the crystal pose were added as inactive poses.
In total, there are 52,385 active and 734,417 inactive poses in the version of Redocked2020 used here, which we have shortened to Redocked.
The PDBBind refined set v.2019 (Z. Liu et al. 2017) is a carefully selected set of high-quality protein-ligand complexes, complete with binding affinities.

In their gnina 1.0 paper (McNutt et al. 2021), the authors took the 4,852 unique protein- ligand complexes, removing solvents and any other molecules besides the protein and the ligand, as well as removing structures with ligands that do not have a mass between 150 and 1,000 Da.
This filtered, preprocessed version of the refined set is hosted by the authors of gnina 1.0 (McNutt et al. 2021).
Of the 4,260 filtered structures, the 441 which are not used in training the ‘redocked’ gnina model were selected as the test set for consistency with that work, which we call gninaSetP ose .
Up to 50 poses are reranked by PointVS (some of which may be very similar), after which the standard 1.0Å RMSD filter was applied to get a final pose ranking.
The PDBBind v.2020 General set contains protein-ligand complexes and binding affinities curated from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) (Berman et al. 2000).
The affinities are in the form of pKd , pKi or pIC50 , and this was the training set for affinity regression.

The PDBBind Core set, also known as the CASF16 test set for affinity regression, comprises 285 high-quality crystal structures, as well as their binding affinities (Su et al. 2019), and is a subset of the General set.
This is the test set for regression (scoring power and ranking power).
Due to the lack of affinity data, we chose to pretrain on a pose classification task in order to learn some of the physics of binding before finetuning on affinity data.

As per Fig 2.1, filtered subsets of both the Redocked set and the PDBBind v.2020 General Set were generated for both of these stages of training, as well as random subsets of the original training sets of the same size as the filtered sets.
The filtered datasets were constructed by removing proteins and ligands if they met either of the following criteria: 1.
Tanimoto similarity of the 2048-bit Morgan fingerprint between the ligand and any of the 285 test set ligands is greater than 0.8 2.
Sequence identity between the protein and any of the 285 test set proteins is greater than 0.8 These filters were also applied to the Redocked set with respect to the gninaSetP ose test set.
All files which could not be parsed by either RDKit (Landrum et al. 2023) or OpenBabel (O’Boyle et al. 2011) were also discarded.
This process reduced the training set sizes from 780,572 to 633,047 (Redocked\gninaSetP ose80 ) and 629,963 (Redocked\Core80 ) and from 19,157 to 14,555 (General\Core80 ).
A full list of datasets is given in Table 2.1.
In order to deconvolute the effects of training set size from the effect of the filters, we also constructed training sets of the same size, randomly sampled from the original training sets.
These are called Redocked\gninaSetP oseR , Redocked \CoreR and General\CoreR .
Carrying out filtering in this way should ensure the PDBBind Core set performance is a more accurate reflection of accuracy on unseen targets and ligands.

A number of previous studies have identified the tendency of MLBSFs to make predictions based on dataset biases rather than an understanding of the physics of binding: dataset clustering and cross-validation have been used to demonstrate that many CNN-based MLBSFs, for instance, are prone to distinguishing binders from non-binders based not on protein-ligand interactions, but on ligand features alone (J. Yang et al. 2020; Wallach et al. 2018; L. Chen et al. 2019; Sieg et al. 2019).
Ensuring that predictive power is diminished in the absence of receptor information in the test set causes at least some receptor information to be used (Scantlebury, Brown, et al. 2020).

However, only directly observing which parts of the input space are used in making predictions can give affirmative proof that machine learning models are learning to identify physical interactions that separate active from inactive poses.

Interpretability in machine learning for pose prediction and virtual screening is an ongoing problem; the architecture of most CNNs causes the concept of individual atoms to be lost as information flows deeper into the network, making them fundamentally unsuitable to attribution at the atomic level.
By contrast, graph-based architectures such as PointVS maintain distinct nodes (atoms) until the final layers.
These, having passed through the entire network, are rich in information and are directly related to the relevant atom in the input.

As the node features are directly attributable to their input atom, and the final pose score is a function of the node features, there is a direct relationship between the atoms and the PointVS score, although there is no incentive during training to localise class contributions on particular atoms.
The edges between atoms can also be probed for how much importance is ascribed to atomic interactions, as an intuitive way to describe non- covalent bonds.
As set out in Fig 2.1, we can also use this knowledge of importance assigned by PointVS to edges to identify important protein atoms for binding.

To check whether PointVS has learnt to identify important binding interactions, and further, whether these can be extracted with attribution, we compare the results of performing attribution on PointVS to those found when using other leading MLBSFs.
We use three approaches for attribution: atom masking, bond masking, and edge attention.
Atom masking Atom masking is a process by which the importance of different atoms can be ascertained.
It is carried out by calculating the difference between the score given when an atom i is removed from the set of input atoms, X, and the score when it is present.
As all architectures of MLBSFs take as input atom information, atom masking can be carried out on any MLBSF.
Bond masking Similar to atom masking, bond masking is a process by which the importance of different bonds can be ascertained.
It is carried out by calculating the difference between the score given when an edge e is removed from the input graph encoding the protein-ligand complex and the score when it is present.

Whilst atom masking can be carried out with CNNs and GNNs alike, bond masking can only be carried out with architectures that take as input not only information about the atoms in the complex, but also information about the connections between atoms.

Graph representations of molecules, which use nodes and node features to describe atoms, and edges and edge features to describe interactions between them, are well-suited to this type of attribution.
CNNs, which take only atom information as input, are not.

Edge attention GNN-based MLBSFs can be built to include an attention-like mechanism, where the edges are given a score between 0 and 1 by a shallow multilayer perceptron (MLP) which takes as input the edge embeddings themselves.
These weights can be thought of as indicating how much each edge is weighted by the network, so attribution can easily be performed by extracting the edge attention weights.
In order to facilitate attribution, PointVS was built to include an attention-like mechanism.

After the edges are assigned attention scores, the edge message passed to the ith node at each layer mi is the sum of connecting edge embeddings mij in the neighbourhood of the node N (i), weighted by this attention score eij , as in Equation 8 in Satorras et. al (Satorras et al. 2022):

We carry out attribution with PointVS as well as two other MLBSFs for comparison: a convolution-based method, gnina (McNutt et al. 2021), and another graph-based model, InteractionGraphNet (Jiang et al. 2021).

Having gone some way to demonstrating that PointVS is able to identify important binding interactions—first by showing that it exhibits competitive performance on virtual screening benchmarks even when trained on a rigorously filtered dataset, and second by showing that attribution analysis identifies bonds in some agreement with a distance-based interaction profiler—we investigated whether such analysis could be used to identify hotspots in binding pockets when supplied with a number of bound structures from fragment screen experiments.

We extracted hotspot maps from PointVS by performing edge attention attribution on fragment screen data, and compared the resulting hotspots to those found using a data-driven approach, the Hotspots API (Curran et al. 2020).

This implements the algorithm described in Radoux et al. 2016, covered in Appendix A.2—briefly, this involves searching the CCDC library of chemical contacts to deduce areas in the binding pocket that contribute disproportionately to binding.
Such areas are known as hotspots.
We then process the output of the API as in Hadfield et al. 2022.
Our first test used the bound structures available for the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro).
Mpro is involved in processing polyproteins pp1a and pp1b of SARS-CoV-2, which are necessary for replication and transcription (Huff et al. 2022).

The dataset available for this target is far more extensive than most targets will benefit from, as it is comprised of not only fragment-like molecules, but also follow-up compounds (Boby et al. 2023).
These follow-up compounds, which have been curated with the specific intention of targetting important protein atoms, consist of closely related compounds with the same basic scaffold.

Intuitively, the presence of high-quality compounds should result in PointVS being able to extract higher-quality hotspots, as the bound ligands were designed to interact with protein atoms that have been experimentally validated to be important.

We used this dataset as a starting point to verify that, given a selection of bound structures, PointVS can be used to identify these important protein atoms in a way that is useful for fragment elaboration.

To ensure that PointVS hotspots are reliable for proteins other than Mpro, we include two further targets in this analysis: SARS-CoV-2 non-structural protein 3 (Mac1) (Schuller et al. 2021), and SARS-CoV-2 non-structural protein 14 (NSP14) (Imprachim et al. 2022).
These both have fragment screen datasets available on fragalysis (XChem @ Diamond 2024).
In both cases, these are considerably smaller than the Mpro dataset, and do not contain follow-up compounds.
We used the fragalysis set of crystal ligand structures to obtain fragments to elaborate on.

To do this, we followed the procedure outlined in Hadfield et al. 2022: we enumerated all cuts of acyclic single bonds that are not part of functional groups, and added a ‘dummy’ atom at the site of the cut.
This atom is where atoms will be added to the fragment.

To assess the generated molecules, we docked them using GOLD (Verdonk, Cole, Hartshorn, et al. 2003), the CCDC’s protein-ligand docking software.
We used the constrained docking functionality—constraining using the fragment, for which we have a crystal structure—from which each molecule receives a score.
We then calculated a ligand efficiency by dividing this score by the number of heavy atoms present in the molecule.
This was to compensate for docking algorithms tendencies to favour larger molecules.
From the ligand efficiency, we derived a standardised ligand efficiency.

This was obtained by standardising the ligand efficiencies of the generated molecules and the ground truth molecule for given fragment-hotspot combination to have zero mean and unit variance (here, ground truth molecule refers to the molecule that was segmented to obtain the test fragment).
We then sorted the standardised ligand efficiencies of the elaborations from highest to lowest scoring, and took the mean of the top α.
In this work, we used α=20: in other words, we only considered the top 20 highest-scoring generated molecules for each fragment-hotspot pairing.

Subtracting the ground truth ligand efficiency value from this value then provides us with ∆SLE20 for every fragment-hotspot pair, so for a given hotspot, we take the mean over the ∆SLE20 s of all the fragments successfully elaborated towards it.

We used this metric as it provides an insight into how the elaboration process when using a particular hotspot has impacted the original molecule’s docking score: a positive ∆SLEα means the top elaborations are improvements on the original molecule, and a negative ∆SLEα shows that the elaboration process has decreased the ligand efficiency with respect to the starting molecule.
